photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white); photographic print
photo.reason: The photo documents Hopi artist Fred Kabotie standing before his own painted murals at the Desert View Watchtower, depicting Hopi ceremonial imagery he created — clear evidence of Hopi artistic practice.

photo.name: Muž v tanečním úboru s náhrdelníky a chřestidly
photo.title: Muž v tanečním úboru s náhrdelníky a chřestidly
photo.reason: This is a documentary photograph of a Hopi Antelope clan priest in ceremonial dress with necklaces, sash, and rattles, photographed at Walpi, Arizona — a genuine ethnographic record of Hopi dress and ritual practice, though miscategorized as "sculpture."

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white with colour); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows five Hopi men walking with snake-hunting sticks, sacks, and traditional dress (kilts, moccasins) in the Arizona desert, documenting Hopi Snake Dance ceremonial practice.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white); photographic print
photo.reason: The photo shows Fred Kabotie, a renowned Hopi artist, painting his own murals in the Desert View Watchtower, with another Hopi man in traditional dress present — documentary evidence of Hopi artistic practice and dress.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white with colour); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows a Hopi child carrying a younger child on her back while climbing a wooden ladder between adobe levels in a Hopi village, Arizona — a documentary image of Hopi daily life and dress.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white); photographic print
photo.reason: The photograph shows Hopi men in dance regalia performing before tourists at the Grand Canyon, a documentary image of their dress and ceremonial practice, which fits the claimed ethnicity even though performed for tourist audiences.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white with colour); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows a Hopi (or Southwestern Pueblo) woman in traditional dress with her child on a mule in front of an adobe dwelling with chile ristras hanging, a genuine documentary scene of daily life in the region. This is a commercial Fred Harvey postcard but depicts authentic Southwestern Native dress and dwelling, fitting documentary photo criteria.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white with colour); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows a Hopi (Moqui) man working a cornfield with a hoe, a documentary photo of daily agricultural life on the Hopi Reservation, matching the claimed ethnicity.

household.name: sikt
household.title: sikt
household.reason: A twilled yucca winnowing/sifting basket collected from a named Hopi maker (Tom Pavatea) at Second Mesa, a well-documented Hopi craft form.

household.name: korg, basket
household.title: korg, basket
household.reason: The image shows a wicker tray basket with a whirlwind design, collected at Oraibi (a Hopi village) in 1930, matching well-documented Hopi basketry techniques and materials.

household.name: korg, basket
household.title: korg, basket
household.reason: A coiled yucca basket plaque with geometric radial pattern, collected at Oraibi (Second Mesa area, Hopi territory) in 1930, matching well-documented Hopi coiled basketry tradition.

ceramic.name: kärl, Lerkärl
ceramic.title: kärl, Lerkärl
ceramic.reason: A polychrome jar with the classic Hopi Sikyatki-revival wing/feather and geometric band design, attributed to Nampeyo family potter Elva Nampeyo, clearly a Hopi-made ceramic vessel.

ceramic.name: kruka, kärl, vessel
ceramic.title: kruka, kärl, vessel
ceramic.reason: A polychrome jar with typical red, yellow/cream, and dark brown geometric decoration, matching Hopi (Moki) pottery traditions documented in the museum's own record and collection history from the 1892-93 Madrid exhibition.

ceramic.name: plate, barrel, plate
ceramic.title: plate, barrel, plate
ceramic.reason: A small yellow-slipped Hopi pottery bowl painted with a stylized face design representing Ha-har-wuq-ti (mother of the Natacka figures), confirmed as Hopi by a specialist researcher (Kelley Hays-Gilpin); this is a characteristic piece of Hopi polychrome pottery.

ceramic.name: vessel
ceramic.title: vessel
ceramic.reason: A polychrome burnished pottery jar with painted bird-head (parrot/eagle) and geometric motifs on cream slip, consistent with classic Hopi Sikyatki-revival pottery traditions.

ceramic.name: sked, ladle
ceramic.title: sked, ladle
ceramic.reason: A ceramic miniature ladle with painted decoration, identified by a specialist researcher (Kelley Hays-Gilpin) as likely Hopi, consistent with Southwest Puebloan pottery traditions and household use.

ceramic.name: kärl, kruka, vessel
ceramic.title: kärl, kruka, vessel
ceramic.reason: A painted earthenware bowl with rounded sides, conical rim nodules, and stylized floral/hook motifs in brown on cream/yellow slip, identified by the museum as Hopi Polacca Polychrome ware, a well-documented Hopi pottery tradition.

ceramic.name: pot, vessel,
ceramic.title: pot, vessel,
ceramic.reason: The vessel is a polychrome jar with red slip and black rain-symbol motifs; museum notes originally listed it as Zuni but a 2009 expert review by Kelley Hays-Gilpin (Hopi ceramics specialist) reattributed it as Hopi Polacca Polychrome ware (1850–1910), a well-documented Hopi pottery type made for trade — this counts as independent evidence supporting the Hopi claim.

sculpture.name: kachina-doll
sculpture.title: kachina-doll
sculpture.reason: A carved and painted wooden kachina doll depicting a Mud Head Clown figure with case mask, protuberances, feathers, and dance costume elements — a well-documented Hopi ritual art form. This directly matches the claimed Hopi attribution.

sculpture.name: Doll
sculpture.title: Figurine
sculpture.reason: This is a painted ceramic figurine of a female figure with the characteristic "squash blossom" whorl hairstyle worn by unmarried Hopi women, a well-documented Hopi craft tradition, consistent with the claimed ethnicity and date.

sculpture.name: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.title: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.reason: This is a carved and painted wooden kachina (katsina) figure with feather headdress, a well-known Hopi ritual carving representing spirit beings, matching the claimed ethnicity and category.

sculpture.name: kachina-doll
sculpture.title: kachina-doll
sculpture.reason: This is a carved wooden kachina doll depicting a Mudhead Clown figure (Koshare-type), a well-documented Hopi ritual/ceremonial carving tradition, matching the museum's detailed description of the mask, protuberances, and dance attire.

sculpture.name: kachina, doll
sculpture.title: kachina, doll
sculpture.reason: This is a carved and painted wooden kachina doll with tablita headdress, cloud-terrace motifs and painted human figures, a classic Hopi ceremonial object well documented in the museum's own comparison to Hopi kachina types.

sculpture.name: figur, Kachinadocka, sculpture, figurine
sculpture.title: figur, Kachinadocka, sculpture, figurine
sculpture.reason: This is a carved and painted Hopi kachina doll (squirrel kachina type) with feather attachments, a well-known Hopi carving tradition used in ritual/educational contexts.

sculpture.name: figur: kachina, Kachina, sculpture, figure
sculpture.title: figur: kachina, Kachina, sculpture, figure
sculpture.reason: A small painted wooden kachina doll with feather tuft, ear paddles, and painted face/body — a classic Hopi carved figure type, matching the museum's description as a miniature kachina.

sculpture.name: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.title: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.reason: A small painted wooden kachina figure with feather tuft, consistent with Hopi kachina doll carving tradition described in the museum's own references (though noted as a type sold commercially, it is still a genuine Hopi craft form).

sculpture.name: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.title: figur: kachina, Kachina, figure, sculpture
sculpture.reason: A small painted wooden kachina figure with feather tuft, matching the museum's description of a 7.6 cm miniature kachina of the type sold by Hopi carvers—this is a classic Hopi ritual/craft object.

jewelry.name: Brosch, smycke
jewelry.title: Brosch, smycke
jewelry.reason: A round silver brooch with an overlay maze/bear-clan motif, documented as made by Eldon James, Second Mesa Hopi, purchased directly at an Indian shop in New Mexico—clear Hopi silverwork.

jewelry.name: smycke, Silverarmband
jewelry.title: smycke, Silverarmband
jewelry.reason: The image shows a silver cuff bracelet with an incised wave/moon-symbol motif, purchased from an all-Indian trading shop in New Mexico and documented as Hopi silverwork, consistent with Southwest Native silversmithing traditions.

jewelry.name: smycke, Brosch
jewelry.title: smycke, Brosch
jewelry.reason: Silver brooch in the shape of a hand with an engraved coiled-snake motif, purchased directly from a Hopi silversmith (Mark Loma, Second Mesa, Arizona) at an All Indian trading shop — a documented Hopi-made silver ornament.

jewelry.name: smycke, Brosch
jewelry.title: smycke, Brosch
jewelry.reason: A round silver brooch with an overlay wind/direction symbol design, purchased directly as Hopi work (attributed to Wayne Seyesvapetewa, Second Mesa Hopi) with a distinctive Hopi silver-overlay technique — clear match to claimed ethnicity.

jewelry.name: Brosch, smycke
jewelry.title: Brosch, smycke
jewelry.reason: A silver brooch in the form of a bird, made using Hopi overlay-style silverwork (dark oxidized recessed areas against polished silver), a technique distinctive to Hopi silversmiths; the bird motif and craftsmanship are consistent with Hopi jewelry traditions.

instruments.name: Drum
instruments.title: Drum
instruments.reason: The image shows a wooden cylindrical drum with rawhide heads laced with sinew, accompanied by its padded beater — a traditional Hopi (Pueblo) ceremonial drum type, matching the museum's attribution and description.

instruments.name: Ah-Yah (rattle)
instruments.title: Ah-Yah
instruments.reason: The image shows a pair of gourd rattles with wooden handles, matching the museum's description of a Hopi "Ah-Yah" rattle used in ceremonial contexts; gourd rattles are a well-documented Hopi/Puebloan instrument type.

instruments.name: Bell
instruments.title: Bell
instruments.reason: A bighorn sheep horn fashioned into a bell/rattle with rawhide hanger, labeled "Moqui" (a historic name for the Hopi people), consistent with Hopi ceremonial use of such implements.

instruments.name: Drum
instruments.title: Drum
instruments.reason: A cylindrical hide-covered drum, a traditional musical instrument type made and used by Hopi and other Southwest Native peoples.

garment.name: vyö
garment.title: vyö
garment.reason: A long handwoven wool belt (vyö) with red ground, black edges, green stripes and a raised diamond-chain pattern down the center, woven from Germantown-type commercial wool yarns — a classic Pueblo/Southwest woven belt type long used by Hopi for ceremonial and everyday dress.

garment.name: Kvinnodräkt, dräkt, dress
garment.title: Kvinnodräkt, dräkt, dress
garment.reason: The image shows a dark indigo woven manta-style dress with red and green edge trim, matching the Hopi woman's traditional wedding/burial dress (owa/manta) woven by men, as described in the museum record.

garment.name: bälte, Band
garment.title: bälte, Band
garment.reason: The image shows a woven wool belt/sash (bälte) with warp-patterned red, green, and white bands and twisted fringe, purchased directly at Hubbell Trading Post in Ganado, Arizona — a well-documented Hopi/Southwest weaving type and sale point, consistent with Hopi-made textile belts worn as garment accessories.

painting-mss.name: akvarell, målning
painting-mss.title: akvarell, målning
painting-mss.reason: A watercolor by a named Hopi artist (Tavahoema) depicting a "Red Lizard" kachina dancer in full ceremonial regalia — a classic Hopi artistic tradition documenting their own katsina dance culture.

painting-mss.name: akvarell, målning, water colour
painting-mss.title: akvarell, målning, water colour
painting-mss.reason: A watercolor painting by Hopi artist K. Tavahoema depicting a "Beard Dancer" kachina figure in traditional regalia, signed by the artist and matching the claimed Hopi ethnicity.

painting-mss.name: akvarell, målning
painting-mss.title: akvarell, målning
painting-mss.reason: A watercolor painting by a Hopi artist (signed "K. Tavahoema, Hopi") depicting a Hopi Snake Dancer holding a snake in his mouth, a well-documented Hopi ceremonial tradition, matching the claimed ethnicity and category.

painting-mss.name: akvarell, målning, water colour
painting-mss.title: akvarell, målning, water colour
painting-mss.reason: A watercolor painting of a Hopi kachina "Corn dancer" figure, signed by K. Tavahoema, a Hopi artist, depicting traditional Hopi ceremonial dress and mask — a well-documented genre of Hopi artistic production.

painting-mss.name: målning, akvarell
painting-mss.title: målning, akvarell
painting-mss.reason: This is a watercolor painting by a Hopi artist (signed "K. Tavaheema Hopi") depicting a Kachina/Rug Dancer figure with full traditional regalia, mask, and ceremonial adornment—a classic subject of Hopi painting tradition.
